title: VOR Radials Without the Vertigo
hook: Which radial are you on? Wrong answer costs you the checkride.

scenes.narration: Thirty seconds, kid. V O R radials. Sixty-year-old technology that still confuses pilots daily. Not you. Not after today.
Radials point FROM the station, like spokes on a wheel. You're always ON one radial — the question is which spoke, and which way you're facing.

Set a course, and the needle shows where that course is relative to you. Golden rule for the C D I: fly TOWARD the needle... but only if your heading roughly matches the course you set. Set it backwards and the needle lies to your face. That's reverse sensing.
That's why I love the H S I — the whole card rotates with your heading, so the needle can't reverse-sense. It's the one instrument that never argues with me. Unlike my examiner in eighty-seven.
Radials point from the station. Match your heading to the course, fly toward the needle. And if the picture makes no sense — check what you twisted before you blame the airplane.
A I M one dash one dash three. Old tech, current reg.

quiz.question: VOR radials are defined as courses...
quiz.explanation: A radial always radiates outward FROM the station — the 090 radial lies due east of the VOR.

quiz.question: You get reverse sensing on a basic CDI when:
choices: The OBS course is roughly opposite your direction of flight
You're too close to the station
quiz.explanation: With the OBS set ~180° from your actual course, the needle deflects away from the course — fly-toward-the-needle becomes wrong.

quiz.question: Why can't a properly set HSI reverse-sense?
choices: The course arrow rotates with the compass card, keeping the picture oriented to your heading
It uses GPS instead of the VOR
quiz.explanation: The HSI overlays the course needle on a heading-slaved card, so the deflection is always shown relative to where you're actually pointed.
